questions.stem: Which of these must be fitted with an AIS Class A under NSR s. 118(1)?
options: A 12 m towboat
A 12 m pleasure craft
A 15 m fishing vessel with no passengers that is not a towboat
A 9 m boat carrying one passenger on sheltered waters
questions.explanation: Section 118(1)(f) requires Class A on towboats of 8 m or more. The pleasure craft is excluded from the 20 m rule, the 15 m fishing vessel is not in the list, and the small passenger boat is covered by the Class A or B rule outside sheltered waters.

questions.stem: A 9 m water taxi carrying 6 passengers is on a near coastal Class 2 voyage. What does s. 118 require?
options: AIS Class A only
No AIS at all
AIS only if it carries more than 12 passengers
AIS Class A or Class B
questions.explanation: Section 118(2) requires Class A or B on a vessel not in s. 118(1), engaged on a voyage other than a sheltered waters voyage, if it is 8 m or more in length and carries a passenger.

questions.stem: In the NSR, what is a 'passenger vessel'?
options: A vessel that carries any passenger
A vessel of 20 m or more
A vessel that carries more than 12 passengers
A vessel that carries more than 50 passengers
questions.explanation: Section 1 defines a passenger vessel as one that carries more than 12 passengers. Carrying more than 50 passengers is a separate Class A trigger in s. 118(1)(b).

questions.stem: Which vessels must have a means of displaying graphically the relative ranges and bearings received by the AIS?
options: Only vessels of 300 GT or more on any voyage
The vessels required to have Class A under s. 118(1)
Only passenger vessels carrying 12 or more passengers
Only vessels on international voyages
questions.explanation: Section 118(3) applies to vessels referred to in s. 118(1), that is, the Class A list.

questions.stem: A Class A AIS and a gyro-compass are both fitted. What does s. 118(4) require?
options: They must be connected so heading is sent to the AIS
The gyro must be switched off while the AIS is transmitting
The AIS must be disconnected from the GNSS input
Nothing, because heading is optional on Class A
questions.explanation: If an AIS Class A is fitted and the vessel also has a transmitting heading device or gyro-compass, they must be connected for transmitting heading to the AIS.

questions.stem: How long before departure must a vessel's required AIS be in operation?
options: Only once the vessel is clear of the dock
At least 5 minutes before departure, and while under way
At least 2 hours before, and until berthed
At least 30 minutes before, and for the whole voyage
questions.explanation: Section 118(5) requires the AIS to be in operation for at least 30 minutes immediately before departure and for the entire duration of the voyage, subject to the exceptions in s. 118(6).

questions.stem: Which three kinds of information does an AIS unit broadcast?
options: Weather, tide and current data
Radar, sonar and depth data
Static, dynamic and voyage data
Crew, cargo and insurance details
questions.explanation: Static data is identity and dimensions, dynamic data is position, time, course over ground and speed, and voyage data is items like destination and ETA (Class A).

questions.stem: On which VHF frequencies does AIS operate?
options: 156.800 MHz (channel 16) and 156.300 MHz (channel 6)
406 MHz and 1.6 GHz
questions.explanation: AIS 1 is 161.975 MHz (channel 87B) and AIS 2 is 162.025 MHz (channel 88B). Channel 16 is the VHF distress channel, 121.5 and 243 MHz are old aeronautical distress frequencies, and 406 MHz is the EPIRB band.

questions.stem: Which statement compares Class A and Class B AIS correctly?
options: Class A sends at higher power and reports faster than Class B
Class B sends at higher power and reports faster than Class A
Both classes report at the same rate and power
Class B is the only class that sends voyage data
questions.explanation: Class A is the more capable unit, with higher power, faster reporting and a guaranteed time slot, and it sends voyage data. Class B is lower power, reports about every 30 seconds and its slot is not guaranteed.

questions.stem: A mate sees no AIS target in the direction of a fog signal and decides nothing is there. What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing, because AIS shows every vessel at sea
AIS cannot be used in fog, so it is blank
Only Class B vessels are invisible on AIS
Not every vessel has AIS on; it never replaces radar and look-out
questions.explanation: AIS shows only vessels that carry it, have it on and send correct data. Rule 5 still requires a proper look-out by all available means.

questions.stem: A 22 m pleasure craft, privately owned, no passengers for hire, on a near coastal voyage. What does NSR s. 118 require?
options: AIS Class A, because it is over 20 m
AIS Class B, because it is over 8 m
Nothing under s. 118(1)(a), which excludes pleasure craft
AIS only if it carries more than 12 passengers at a time
questions.explanation: Section 118(1)(a) covers vessels of 20 m or more other than pleasure crafts. Unless another paragraph applies (such as IMDG goods or bulk pollutants), a pleasure craft is outside s. 118.
